**Desire Lines**

There is a term that landscape architects use, half in admiration and half in exasperation, for the paths people wear into the ground when the paved ones don't suit them. They call them desire lines. You have seen them everywhere: the diagonal scar across a university quad, the shortcut through a hedge gap behind a bus shelter, the trampled bare earth that cuts the corner of a right-angled sidewalk. Somebody drew a plan. Somebody else, many somebodies, walked where they wanted instead. The grass gave up, and the ground recorded the disagreement.

I find that I think about desire lines more than the subject probably deserves. Part of it is the name, which is better than the thing. "Desire line" sounds like it belongs in a poem or a psychoanalyst's notebook, not a municipal planning document. But part of it is that the phenomenon seems to me one of the purest available demonstrations of a particular kind of truth: the truth that is not stated by anyone, that no single person would defend, and that is nevertheless written plainly on the earth for anyone who cares to read it.

No one decides to make a desire line. That is the essential thing. The first person to step off the pavement onto the lawn was not founding anything. They were late, or they were carrying groceries, or they simply saw that the angle was wrong and their feet corrected it before their conscience could object. The second person, a few hours later, might have noticed a slight flattening of the grass and taken it as a kind of permission. By the hundredth person there was a visible path, and by the thousandth there was mud, and at some point a groundskeeper stood over it with a rake and a look of resignation. Each individual act was trivial, forgettable, almost involuntary. The aggregate is a statement so clear it may as well be carved in stone: *the path is in the wrong place.*

I love this because it inverts the usual relationship between intention and meaning. We tend to assume that the things that mean the most are the things people meant the most. A manifesto means more than a shopping list. A wedding vow means more than a grunt of assent. But the desire line means precisely because no one meant it. It cannot lie. It cannot posture. It cannot have been drafted by a committee eager to appear a certain way. It is the residue of ten thousand small honesties, each of them the honesty of a body that would rather not walk farther than it has to.

---

There is a story, probably apocryphal in its details but true in spirit, about a university that built a new campus and refused to lay any footpaths for the first year. They planted grass and let the students walk. When the desire lines appeared, they paved them. I have heard this attributed to several universities, which is usually a sign that it happened at none of them and that everyone wishes it had. The story is attractive for the same reason the desire line itself is attractive: it suggests a kind of humility on the part of the designer. It says, I do not know where you want to go. I will wait and let you tell me with your feet.

Most design does not work this way, and probably most design cannot. You cannot let people walk across a bridge before you build it in order to find out where the bridge should go. There are constraints that precede use. But I think the fantasy of the patient university is a fantasy about a particular relationship to knowledge, and it is worth taking seriously even if the story is false. It is the fantasy that the world already contains the answer to many of our questions and that our job is not so much to decide as to notice.

Consider how much of what we call expertise is really this kind of noticing. A good editor does not impose structure on a manuscript so much as find the structure the manuscript is already reaching toward and clear away what is blocking it. A good teacher does not pour knowledge into a student but observes where the student's attention naturally goes and builds the path there. A good doctor, at least in the old ideal, listens to the patient describe the ache before running the tests, because the patient's body has already been wearing a track through the grass for months. In all of these cases the expert's skill is not primarily in the deciding but in the reading, and what is being read is a kind of desire line: a pattern worn into some substrate by repeated, unconsidered, honest pressure.

---

But I want to be careful not to romanticize this too much, because desire lines are also frequently stupid.

The shortcut across the lawn saves eleven seconds and destroys a patch of grass that took a season to establish. The gap in the hedge lets pedestrians through and also lets in the wind that kills the roses. The diagonal path across the quad is, from the point of view of the person taking it, obviously correct, and from the point of view of anyone who has to look at the quad, an eyesore. Desire lines represent the aggregate of individual local optimizations, and individual local optimizations are notoriously bad at producing good collective outcomes. That is more or less the definition of a tragedy of the commons. Every person who cuts the corner is right, and the result is wrong.

So the desire line is honest, but honesty is not the same as wisdom. It tells you what people want. It does not tell you whether they should have it. The planner who refuses to pave the diagonal is not necessarily a fool or a tyrant; she may have seen something the walkers didn't, some reason the paths were laid at right angles that had to do with drainage or sightlines or the simple fact that a quad with a diagonal slash across it looks like a mistake. The walkers, for their part, are not necessarily wise; they are just tired, and tiredness has its own imperatives that have nothing to do with the good of the whole.

What interests me is that both sides are in possession of a real truth and neither is in possession of the whole truth. The walker knows something the planner does not: that the angle is wrong, that the body rejects it, that no amount of paving will make people take the long way around when the short way is right there. The planner knows something the walker does not: what the corner-cutting costs, what the space is for, why the grass matters. The desire line is where these two knowledges collide, and the mud is the record of neither side winning.

I think this is a fairly common shape for disagreements to take, once you start looking for it. One party has the knowledge of use and the other has the knowledge of design. One knows how things feel from the inside and the other knows how they fit together from above. Each is tempted to dismiss the other's knowledge as illegitimate—the planner thinks the walkers are lazy, the walkers think the planner is out of touch—when in fact both are simply reporting from different vantage points about the same stretch of ground. The hard thing, the thing almost no one manages, is to hold both reports at once and let them argue.

---

There is a version of the desire line that exists in language. Linguists call it, less poetically, usage. The rule says one thing; the speakers do another; eventually the rule gives way. For centuries English grammarians insisted that you could not end a sentence with a preposition, that you could not split an infinitive, that "whom" must be used in the objective case. For centuries English speakers ignored them, not out of rebellion but because the rules were in the wrong place and the body of the language would not walk that way. Now the grammarians have mostly paved the diagonal. Nobody decided this. It was worn in.

I find this comforting in a way that is hard to articulate. It means the language belongs to the people who use it and not to the people who describe it, and that the describers, if they are honest, will eventually catch up. But it also means that every complaint about declining standards, every letter to the editor about the misuse of "literally," is a groundskeeper standing over a muddy track with a rake. The groundskeeper is not wrong that the grass is ruined. He is just wrong about who is in charge of where people walk.

And yet—here the caution returns—the fact that a usage is widespread does not make it good. There are desire lines in language that lead nowhere useful. There are words that have been worn into mush by overuse until they carry no meaning at all, and the wearing was as unconsidered and as collectively honest as any lawn shortcut. "Literally" is a case in point: the people who use it to mean "figuratively" are not wrong about anything, they are just walking where their feet take them, and where their feet take them is toward a word that no longer distinguishes between the thing that happened and the thing that felt like it happened. That is a real loss. It is also probably irreversible. Both of those things are true, and the person who insists on only one of them is missing half the picture.

---

I said earlier that a desire line cannot lie, and I want to hold onto that while also complicating it, because I think there is a sense in which a desire line can mislead even though it cannot deceive.

Here is what I mean. The path across the quad says: people want to get from this door to that door by the shortest route. That is true. But it does not say why they want to get there, or whether they would still want to if the doors were somewhere else, or whether the shortness is really what they care about or just what they settle for. It records the desire but not its origin. If the building on the far side of the quad were moved, the path would vanish overnight, and no one would mourn it. The desire line is a symptom, and symptoms are honest without being explanatory.

This matters because the temptation, once you have learned to read desire lines, is to treat them as oracles. To pave every diagonal, to accept every usage, to build whatever the aggregate of unconsidered behavior seems to be asking for. And this is its own kind of laziness—the laziness of the designer who wants to be relieved of the burden of judgment, who would rather follow the mud than think about where the mud should be. The patient university in the story is admirable not because it gave up deciding but because it waited to decide until it had more information. Waiting is not the same as abdicating. The grass was still theirs. The choice of what to pave was still theirs. They just declined to make it blind.

I suspect the best designers, in any field, are the ones who hold this tension well. They read the desire lines carefully and take them seriously as evidence, but they do not mistake evidence for verdict. They ask what the path is really saying—not just where people walk but why, and what would make them walk elsewhere, and whether the thing they are walking toward is worth reaching. They pave some diagonals and refuse others, and they can tell you the reason in each case. This is much harder than either ignoring the walkers or obeying them, and it is, I think, the only approach that respects both the knowledge of use and the knowledge of design.

---

I want to end somewhere more personal, because the reason I think about desire lines is not really that I care about landscape architecture.

It is that I am often uncertain what I want, and the desire line offers a model for finding out that does not require me to already know. I cannot always say, in advance, what I would choose. I can only notice, over time, where I keep ending up. The book I keep returning to. The question I keep circling. The friend I call when something has gone wrong, as opposed to the friend I tell myself I ought to call. These are paths worn into a lawn I did not plant, by feet I did not consciously direct, and they tell me things about myself that my stated preferences do not. They are more honest than my intentions and less articulate. They cannot lie, and they cannot explain.

The work, then, is the same as the planner's. Read the mud. Take it seriously. Do not assume that because a path is there it should be paved—some of my desire lines lead to places I should not keep going—but do not assume either that the right-angled sidewalks of my stated values are where I actually live. Hold both. Let them argue. And be humble enough to wait, sometimes, before deciding which one to believe.

There is a patch of grass outside a building I used to walk past every day, and across it a diagonal path had been worn so deep it was almost a trench. One spring the groundskeepers finally paved it. I remember feeling an odd mix of satisfaction and loss—satisfaction that the truth had been acknowledged, loss that the acknowledgment had erased the evidence. The paved path was correct, and it was also mute. It no longer said anything. It was just a path. Whereas the mud had been a kind of speech, ten thousand people's worth, none of whom had meant to say anything at all.

I don't know what to make of that. Perhaps only that some truths are most visible while they are still being contested, and that the resolution of the argument, however welcome, always costs us the argument itself. The grass will not grow back over the pavement. The record is sealed. Somewhere else, on some other lawn, someone is stepping off the sidewalk for the first time, and the ground is beginning, very quietly, to take notes.
